text:
A: Helloooo! Oh, there you are. I'm Ceri, sorry, my laptop's been playing up.
B: Hiya, I'm Gemma! No, you're fine, I could hear you. How's your day going?
A: Oh, not bad, ta. Knackered, mind. I've been on placement all week. Where are you then? You sound northern.
B: Warrington. Sort of between Manchester and Liverpool, so I get told I sound like both and neither. And you're Welsh, obviously!
A: Pontypridd, born and bred. Ponty. Is that your dog in the corner of your photo? I could see a tail.
B: That's Bonnie, my Labrador. She ate a sock last month, a whole sock, and we had to go to the vet. Cost a fortune. She's absolutely fine now, not sorry in the slightest.
A: Oh, they never are! Mine's Bwbach, old Staffie, snores like a tractor. He's on the settee now, you can probably hear him in a minute.
B: Ah, bless him. What's the placement, if you don't mind me asking?
A: So I'm doing occupational therapy at Cardiff. Second year. I'm a mature student, I'm forty-one, so I'm about twenty years older than everyone else on the course, which is a laugh. Before that I was a hairdresser for, God, twenty years.
B: Oh, that's brilliant though. I'm forty, so we're the same sort of age. I think that's dead brave, going back.
A: Brave or daft, depends who you ask! The essays are killing me, mind. The anatomy I love, the writing, not so much. I've got one due Friday and I haven't started it.
B: Oh no! Well, I'm the opposite, I can't leave anything. I do the accounts and admin for a scaffolding firm, and I'll have the timesheets reconciled a day early. The lads in the yard think I'm mad.
A: I need you living with me, honestly. Colour-coded, are you?
B: Oh, the diary's colour-coded, the calendar's colour-coded. My husband says if it's not on the calendar it's not happening. Sorry, am I waffling?
A: No, you're lush, carry on! I do colour-coded notes when I'm stressed, then I don't look at them. What's the scaffolding place like?
B: It's nice actually, it's family-run, so I sort of know everyone. Bit of mithering on the phone chasing invoices, but I don't mind that, you know. I'm quite polite but I don't let them off.
A: Fair play. That's like doing a client's colour, isn't it? You're all nice and chatty, then you tell them no, you can't go platinum from black in one go.
B: Ha, I'd have been one of them, to be fair! So what got you into OT? Was it a big change?
A: Erm, my dad had a stroke about three years back. And the OTs who came to the house were amazing, getting him back doing his own cup of tea and that. And I thought, I could do that. Talking to people is my whole job anyway, twenty years of salon chat.
B: Oh, I'm sorry about your dad. That's lovely though, that you saw it and went for it. Is he doing alright?
A: He's doing tidy, yeah. Slower, but he's still bossing Mam around. What about you, do you do much outside work?
B: Netball on a Tuesday, back-to-netball, I'm goal defence. And parkrun on a Saturday, but I'm slow, I mostly go for the chat and a barm after. Well, not every week, sorry, most weeks.
A: A what after?
B: A barm! A bread roll, like a bacon barm. Do you not say that?
A: No! It's a roll, love, or a bap. Barm. I'm stealing that, I'm saying that to Dai tonight at tea and he'll think I've gone
